summary: Describes Secure HTTP, a way to protect messages sent over HTTP with confidentiality, authenticity and integrity, and non-repudiation. It is historic; most of the web later used TLS instead.

eli5.summary: A way to put web messages in locked envelopes. The world chose a different lock, so this one is now mostly a history lesson.

what is the secure method in s-http
subtitle: A way to sign, authenticate and encrypt individual HTTP messages, with the protections negotiated for each transaction.

tldr.problem: The original HTTP had only modest support for the cryptography that commercial web transactions need, such as authenticating both sides and keeping sensitive data confidential.
tldr.mechanism: S-HTTP wraps a whole HTTP message inside a secured message sent with a special Secure method. The wrapper can add a signature, a keyed-hash authenticator or encryption, and each party states its cryptographic preferences in negotiation headers.
tldr.outcome: It is a message-level design with very flexible options. It is now marked Historic, and the RFC itself was published as an Experimental protocol.

today: RFC 2660 is marked Historic and has not been obsoleted by another RFC. It was published as an Experimental protocol.

sections.title: Why Secure HTTP
sections.content:
Many web applications need the client and server to authenticate each other and exchange sensitive information confidentially. Secure HTTP (S-HTTP) is a message-oriented protocol designed to coexist with HTTP's messaging model, giving equal treatment to requests and replies. The aim is to support spontaneous commercial transactions, with a choice of operation modes, key management mechanisms, trust models, cryptographic algorithms and message formats negotiated for each transaction.

S-HTTP-aware clients can talk to servers that do not know it, and the reverse, although such transactions use no S-HTTP security. It does not need client-side public key certificates, since it supports modes that use only symmetric keys. The RFC says it differs from Digest Authentication (RFC 2617) by supporting public key cryptography and digital signatures as well as confidentiality.

This document describes S-HTTP/1.4, which adds support for the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) and with it the Diffie-Hellman and NIST Digital Signature Standard cryptosystems.
sections.eli5: Early web messages travelled like open postcards. S-HTTP lets two computers put them in envelopes that can be sealed, signed or both, without first needing a fancy ID for everyone.

sections.title: Processing Model and Modes of Protection
sections.content:
Making an S-HTTP message takes three inputs: the cleartext message (an HTTP message or another data object), the receiver's cryptographic preferences and keying material, and the sender's own. The sender combines the preferences and applies the resulting enhancements. The receiver reads the headers to learn which transformations were applied, removes them, and may check they match what was promised and requested.

Protection works on three independent axes: signature, authentication and encryption. A message may use any combination, including none. Encryption keys can be sent in a public-key envelope, or can be prearranged symmetric keys identified in a header line. The authentication mode uses a Message Authentication Code, a keyed hash over the document computed with a shared secret, with no public key cryptography or encryption needed. The designers deliberately left explicit signing for conscious use, since much authentication, such as access control, needs only the lighter MAC.

A challenge-response nonce mechanism lets the parties check freshness. Because headers are integrity-protected, the HTTP Date: header may also serve as a freshness indicator.
sections.eli5: You can mix and match three protections: sign the envelope, stamp it with a secret handshake, or lock it. Each one can be used alone or together, depending on what the two sides need.

sections.title: Message Format
sections.content:
S-HTTP messages look like HTTP: a request or status line, headers, and a body. The request line uses the special Secure method and the designator Secure-HTTP/1.4, with the Request-URI normally just an asterisk so no sensitive information leaks. That means S-HTTP and HTTP can be mixed on one TCP port, for example port 80. Responses should use Secure-HTTP/1.4 and always the status 200 OK if the S-HTTP processing succeeded, because the real result of the wrapped request is only visible inside.

Only Content-Type and Content-Privacy-Domain are required headers. The privacy domain is CMS or MOSS. Other headers include Prearranged-Key-Info for keys arranged outside the format, and MAC-Info, which carries a MAC. The new MAC construction in this memo is derived from HMAC (RFC 2104), and the older constructions are kept for backwards compatibility.

After the wrapper is removed, the content should be a normal HTTP request or response, shown as message/http, or another S-HTTP message. That recursive wrapping lets signed and enveloped enhancements be layered, and lets a proxy apply or remove protection for itself.
sections.eli5: An S-HTTP message looks like a normal web message on the outside, but its label is generic and the answer is always 'OK'. The real request and the real answer stay hidden in the envelope.

sections.title: Negotiating Cryptographic Options
sections.content:
Each party can state what it requires, allows or refuses. A negotiation header is a list of specifications with a property (such as the bulk encryption algorithm), a value (such as DES-CBC), a direction and a strength. The key is written as a mode, orig or recv, joined to an action: optional, required or refused. For example, SHTTP-Symmetric-Content-Algorithms: recv-optional=DES-CBC,RC2 says the sender may use either cipher for messages to this party. Optional values are listed in decreasing order of preference.

These headers go in the encapsulated HTTP headers, not the outer S-HTTP headers. Besides the privacy domain, they cover certificate types, key exchange algorithms (DH, RSA, Inband, Outband), signature algorithms (RSA, NIST-DSS), message digest algorithms and symmetric ciphers. Non-negotiation headers such as Key-Assign, Certificate-Info and Nonce supply keying material and freshness values. An agent that finds the other side incompatible may end the connection or return Not implemented 501.
sections.eli5: Before sending, each side hands the other a wish list: 'I need this, this is fine, never that.' The two then pick something that suits both.

sections.title: Retries and Security Errors
sections.content:
A server may reject a request while hinting that a retry with different cryptographic options could work, for instance because a link's old page did not require a signature but server policy now does. The new options are carried in the header of the encapsulated reply. The guiding principle is that the user should get the same informed choice as in a normal link click, and a client must not sign a request without asking permission.

The RFC defines new status codes. 420 SecurityRetry says a retry with different enhancements is worth trying, and also covers a plain HTTP request that should have been S-HTTP. 421 BogusHeader reports a bad S-HTTP request. Servers should answer clear requests that need protection with 420. A new URL scheme, shttp, marks targets that are S-HTTP capable, so S-HTTP-unaware clients do not send sensitive data in the clear.
sections.eli5: If the server says 'try again with a stronger lock', your browser should ask you before it does anything like signing your name.

sections.title: Required Algorithms and Security Notes
sections.content:
Every S-HTTP agent must support the MD5 message digest and MAC authentication, and, as of S-HTTP/1.4, the RSA-MD5-HMAC construction. Agents must support Outband, Inband and DH key exchange, encryption with DES-CBC, and signature generation and verification with NIST-DSS.

The Security Considerations section says only that the entire document is about security. The RFC also notes that the MAC mode gives integrity and sender authentication without non-repudiation, and that an inband key must travel inside the secured request, so it cannot be used in unencrypted messages.
sections.eli5: The rule book lists the few locks every S-HTTP program has to know, so that any two of them can find at least one way to talk securely.

items.label: Receive: optional
items.desc: Will process the enhancement if used, and also messages without it.

items.label: Receive: required
items.desc: Will not process messages without this enhancement.

items.label: Receive: refused
items.desc: Will not process messages with this enhancement.

items.label: Originate: optional
items.desc: Provides it only when the other side requires it.
